incidents.title: User updates profile and refreshes immediately
incidents.brief: The primary database accepts a profile update, but a read goes to a replica that is still stale.
incidents.constraint: Replication is asynchronous and users expect freshness.
incidents.question: What keeps the experience correct?

choices.label: Route the writer's reads to the primary for a few seconds
choices.resultTitle: The writer sees their update at once
choices.resultBody: For a few seconds after a write, only that user's reads go to the primary; everyone else stays on replicas, so their refresh shows the new profile and primary load barely moves.

choices.label: Block all reads until replication catches up
choices.resultBody: Blocking reads until replication catches up stalls all 4,000 req/s, not just the writer's refresh; p95 climbs to 1 s and 40 requests error out.

choices.label: Disable the replicas and send every read to the primary
choices.resultBody: The writer now sees fresh data, but all 4,000 req/s land on the primary; p95 stays near 880 ms and 20 requests error while its connection pool queues.

hints: The writer expects their own update.
Replicas can lag.
Use a fresh read path.

incidents.title: Authors see their old draft after saving
incidents.brief: Postly takes 900 saves/s and serves 40k reads/s from 3 async replicas lagging 0.3-4 s. 18% of authors refresh, see the pre-edit draft, and re-save it over their own changes.
incidents.constraint: The primary is at 82% CPU and cannot absorb the authors' 12k reads/s.
incidents.question: How does an author always see their own save without loading the primary?

choices.label: Session keeps commit LSN; read only caught-up replicas

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Read-your-writes per session; other readers stay eventually consistent.

choices.resultBody: Each save returns the primary's commit LSN, stored in the session. The router sends that author's reads only to a replica whose replay LSN has passed it, and falls back to the primary only when none has. Old-draft views drop to 0% while primary CPU barely moves. Cost: the router polls replica replay positions every 100 ms.

choices.label: Pin each author's reads to the primary for 60 seconds
choices.resultBody: Authors are 30% of sessions and read heavily inside the editor, so about 12k reads/s land on a primary already at 82%. CPU hits 97%, save p95 climbs from 40 ms to 900 ms, and saves start timing out.

choices.label: Switch all three replicas to synchronous_commit remote_apply
choices.resultTitle: Every save waits on the slowest replica
choices.resultBody: Commits now wait until all three replicas have applied the WAL, so save latency tracks the 4 s straggler during its vacuum runs. Save p95 rises to 3.8 s, and a single replica restart blocks every write.

hints: Authors only need to see their own writes, not everyone else's.
Each replica knows exactly how far it has replayed the primary's log.
What if the session remembered where its last write landed in the WAL?

incidents.title: Confirmed bookings vanish after failover
incidents.brief: Reservo's us-east primary died and failover promoted the us-west async replica, 6 s behind. 1,900 confirmed bookings vanished; diners arrived at restaurants with no reservation.
incidents.constraint: Booking writes must stay under 25 ms p99, and us-west is 70 ms away.
incidents.question: How do you make failover keep every acknowledged booking?

choices.label: Semi-sync standby in the same region, promoted first

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Zero loss for in-region failures; a full-region loss can still drop the async tail.

choices.resultBody: Each commit now waits for an in-region standby, about 1 ms away, to persist the WAL before acknowledging. A primary crash loses nothing that was confirmed, and failover promotes that standby. The us-west replica stays async for regional disasters. Cost: +2 ms write p99 and one more database server.

choices.label: Cut failover detection from 30 s to 5 s with tighter probes
choices.resultTitle: Failover is faster, bookings still gone
choices.resultBody: The app is back in 8 s instead of 35 s, but the promoted node still only has what us-west had replayed. The 6 s of async lag, about 1,900 bookings at peak, is lost on every failover.

choices.label: Make replication to the us-west replica fully synchronous
choices.resultTitle: Every booking pays a 70 ms round trip
choices.resultBody: Nothing acknowledged is lost any more, but every commit now waits for a cross-country round trip. Write p99 jumps from 12 ms to 150 ms, blowing the 25 ms budget, and any WAN blip stalls all bookings.

hints: Failing over quickly and failing over without data loss are different problems.
Anything acknowledged but not yet on the promoted node is gone.
Some copy close enough to wait on cheaply must hold the log before the ack.

incidents.title: Support agents refund the same order twice
incidents.brief: Shiply agents refund orders in Postgres, but the console lists orders from Elasticsearch, fed by CDC with a 30 s refresh. 22% of refunds get issued twice because the order still says 'paid'.
incidents.constraint: The index ingests 25k updates/s; refreshing faster than every 30 s overloads it.
incidents.question: How do agents see the refund they just issued?

choices.label: Read order detail from Postgres by ID; search via index

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Source of truth for decisions; the derived index stays eventually consistent.

choices.resultTitle: Order page shows the refund instantly
choices.resultBody: Search still finds orders through the index, but opening an order now reads its row from Postgres by primary key, about 2 ms. Agents see 'refunded' immediately and double refunds drop to 0 while the index keeps its 30 s refresh. Cost: one extra DB read per order view, about 300 reads/s.

choices.label: Drop the Elasticsearch refresh interval from 30 s to 1 s
choices.resultTitle: Index cluster buckles under segment merges
choices.resultBody: Refreshing 30 times more often creates tiny segments that must be merged constantly. At 25k updates/s the index CPU hits 98%, CDC lag grows to 90 s, and agents now see even older statuses.

choices.label: Dual-write each refund to Postgres and Elasticsearch together
choices.resultTitle: Direct index writes still hide for 30 s
choices.resultBody: The direct write is invisible until the next 30 s refresh anyway, so double refunds barely fall. Worse, when the index write times out (0.4% of calls) or races the CDC event, the two stores drift and 3% of orders show the wrong state permanently.

hints: Search indexes are built for finding things, not for being current.
The index is a derived copy that trails its source by at least one refresh.
Which store should answer 'what is this one order's state right now'?

incidents.title: Commenters post the same reply twice
incidents.brief: Forumly caches thread pages at the CDN for 60 s, serving 95k req/s at a 97% hit ratio. After posting, commenters don't see their reply, so 9% of comments are duplicates.
incidents.constraint: Origin handles at most 8k req/s; the hit ratio must stay above 90%.
incidents.question: How does a new comment show up without giving up the CDN?

choices.label: Purge the thread's surrogate key on each new comment

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Sub-second staleness after writes; still a shared cache the rest of the time.

choices.resultTitle: Threads refresh within a second of a reply
choices.resultBody: Each thread page is tagged with a surrogate key, and the comment handler fires a purge for that key, which reaches all POPs in about 150 ms. The next request refills from origin, so the commenter and everyone else see the reply. Hit ratio dips to 95% on busy threads. Cost: purges are rate-limited by the CDN API, so hot threads need batching.

choices.label: Drop the CDN thread-page TTL from 60 seconds to 2 s
choices.resultBody: Commenters still wait up to 2 s, and the long tail of quiet threads now misses constantly. Hit ratio falls to 78%, about 21k req/s reach an origin sized for 8k, and p95 climbs to 2.4 s.

choices.label: Bypass the CDN cache for all logged-in readers
choices.resultBody: Logged-in readers are 35% of traffic, so 33k req/s now hit an origin sized for 8k. CPU pegs at 99% and p95 reaches 3 s. Commenters would see their reply, if the page loaded at all.

hints: The cached copy is only wrong right after something changes.
You know exactly which page a new comment changes.
Could the write itself tell the CDN to drop that one page?

incidents.title: Items vanish from shared shopping lists
incidents.brief: Listo runs active-active in EU and US. Households edit shared lists from both, and rows merge last-writer-wins on wall-clock time. 6% of concurrent adds vanish, more when a node drifts 400 ms.
incidents.constraint: Each region must keep accepting writes through a 10-minute transatlantic partition.
incidents.question: How do concurrent edits from two regions both survive?

choices.label: Model each list as an OR-Set CRDT merged per item

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Convergent merges with no coordination; semantics are add-wins, not arbitrary.

choices.resultTitle: Both regions' adds survive the merge
choices.resultBody: Every add carries a unique tag and a remove only cancels tags it has seen, so replicas converge to the union of concurrent adds regardless of clocks or arrival order. Lost adds fall to 0 and partitions heal on their own. Cost: tombstone metadata, about 40 bytes per removed item until compaction.

choices.label: Run PTP-grade clock sync so skew stays under 5 ms
choices.resultTitle: Fewer skew losses, concurrent adds still lost
choices.resultBody: Better clocks stop the drifting node from winning unfairly, but two adds inside the 180 ms replication window still overwrite the same list row and LWW keeps only one. Lost adds fall from 6% to 4.5%.

choices.label: Route every list's writes to a single home region
choices.resultTitle: The partition takes half the users offline
choices.resultBody: With a single writable region there are no conflicts, but US households pay 90 ms extra per edit. During the partition every household homed across the Atlantic gets write errors, breaking the availability requirement.

hints: The bug isn't the clock; it's that one write replaces the other.
Adding two different items to a list isn't really a conflict.
Some data types merge concurrent updates correctly by construction.

incidents.title: Deleted pins come back after a node rejoins
incidents.brief: A Pinbo Cassandra node was down 12 days, then rejoined. gc_grace_seconds is 10 days, so its peers had purged their tombstones; 31k deleted pins, including legal takedowns, reappeared.
incidents.constraint: Hardware swaps can keep a node offline for up to 2 weeks.
incidents.question: What keeps deleted pins deleted?

choices.label: Rebuild nodes offline past gc_grace; repair inside it

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Anti-entropy runs on a schedule tied to tombstone lifetime.

choices.resultBody: A node offline longer than gc_grace_seconds is now wiped and re-streamed instead of rejoining with its old data, and incremental repair finishes every 5 days, well inside the 10-day window, so every replica sees each tombstone before it is purged. Cost: a rebuild streams about 2 TB and takes 6 hours.

choices.label: Lower gc_grace_seconds to 1 day so tombstones purge sooner
choices.resultTitle: Tombstones expire before repair reaches them
choices.resultBody: Tombstones now disappear after one day, so any replica that misses a delete for longer than that, even a short outage plus a slow repair, brings the data back. Resurrections go from rare events to a weekly occurrence.

choices.label: Require ALL replicas to acknowledge each delete
choices.resultTitle: Deletes fail whenever a node is down
choices.resultBody: ALL makes every replica acknowledge the tombstone, so during Node C's 12-day absence every delete touching its token ranges fails, including legal takedowns. A third of deletes error out and the retry backlog grows to 40k.

hints: In Cassandra a delete is just another write, called a tombstone.
Tombstones are only kept for gc_grace_seconds, then compacted away.
A replica that never saw the tombstone still holds the live value.

incidents.title: Profile edits appear to revert for a minute
incidents.brief: Quilt writes a profile to the primary, then deletes its Redis key. A concurrent miss refills the key from a replica 800 ms behind, caching the old profile for the full 60 s TTL. 3% of edits look reverted.
incidents.constraint: Cache misses must keep reading replicas; the primary is at 80% CPU.
incidents.question: How do you stop a stale refill from outliving the write?

choices.label: Write through with a version; fills only set if newer

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Cache never moves backwards; staleness limited to replica lag on cold keys.

choices.resultBody: The writer now SETs the new profile with its row version, and cache fills go through a Lua script that only writes if their version is higher than the cached one. The 800 ms-stale replica read loses and is dropped. Reverted edits fall to 0.02%, only after evictions. Cost: a version per entry and a script call per fill.

choices.label: Shorten the profile cache TTL from 60 s to 5 s
choices.resultTitle: Stale window shrinks, hit ratio collapses
choices.resultBody: Stale profiles now last 5 s instead of 60 s, but most profiles are read less than once every 5 s. Hit ratio falls from 94% to 61%, replica CPU climbs to 88%, and reverted edits still show up 1% of the time.

choices.label: Delete the Redis key before writing the database, not after
choices.resultBody: Deleting first opens a gap before the commit: any reader in that window refills the cache with pre-write data, and then the write lands underneath it. Reverted edits rise from 3% to 5%.

hints: The delete works. Something puts the old value back afterwards.
The refill reads from a replica that hasn't seen the write yet.
What if the cache could tell an older value from a newer one?

incidents.title: Authors can't find the post they just made
incidents.brief: Chirp fans each post out to followers' timelines through a queue. At peak the backlog reaches 45 s, so authors reload, don't see their own post, and 12% post it again.
incidents.constraint: Accounts with 3M followers post during live events; fanout cannot move into the request.
incidents.question: How does an author see their own post immediately?

choices.label: Merge the author's own recent posts into their timeline

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Read-your-writes for authors; followers stay eventually consistent.

choices.resultBody: A timeline read now unions the cached timeline with the author's last 20 posts from the posts table, an indexed read of about 1 ms. The author sees the post at once while followers still receive it through fanout. Duplicate posts drop to 0.3%. Cost: one extra read per timeline load.

choices.label: Double the fanout worker fleet so the queue drains faster
choices.resultTitle: Backlog clears until the next celebrity post
choices.resultBody: Everyday backlog drops to 8 s, but a single 3M-follower post still enqueues 3M timeline writes and the backlog spikes to 40 s during live events. Authors keep missing their posts exactly when traffic peaks, and the fleet costs twice as much.

choices.label: Fan out to all followers synchronously before POST returns
choices.resultTitle: Celebrity posts take a minute to save
choices.resultBody: A 3M-follower post now waits for 3M timeline writes inside the request. POST latency reaches 60 s and requests time out, so the post is saved but the client shows an error and retries, creating even more duplicates.

hints: The author is one reader; the followers are millions.
Fanout exists to build other people's timelines.
The author's own posts are cheap to find directly.

incidents.title: Saved settings revert when the network changes
incidents.brief: Trippo's GeoDNS sends users to us-east or us-west by carrier egress, which flips mid-session. A setting saved in one region reads stale from the other for 1.5 s; 14% of edits appear to revert.
incidents.constraint: Each user's data is homed in one region; the other region serves async copies.
incidents.question: How do reads in the other region honor a user's last write?

choices.label: Cookie carries write position; lagging region proxies home

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Read-your-writes across regions, paid only by recently-writing sessions.

choices.resultTitle: Cross-region reads honor the last write
choices.resultBody: After a write, the session cookie carries the home region and the commit position. A region whose copy is behind that position proxies the read to the home region, adding 70 ms to about 2% of reads; everyone else reads locally. Reverted edits drop to 0.

choices.label: Lower the GeoDNS record TTL from 300 s to 30 s
choices.resultTitle: Users flip regions even more often
choices.resultBody: Shorter TTLs make resolvers re-query more often, so a carrier egress change moves users across regions sooner and more frequently. Reverted edits rise from 14% to 17%.

choices.label: Replicate every write synchronously to both US regions
choices.resultTitle: Every write pays the coast-to-coast trip
choices.resultBody: Reverts stop, but every write in the app now waits about 70 ms for the other coast. Write p99 goes from 20 ms to 160 ms, and any blip on the cross-region link stalls all writes.

hints: The user didn't change; the region answering them did.
Only sessions that just wrote something need fresher data.
The request could carry proof of how new its data must be.

incidents.title: Two teams booked into the same meeting room
incidents.brief: Deskly checks for an overlapping booking, then inserts, inside one REPEATABLE READ transaction. Two users booking Room 4B for 10:00 both see it free and both commit: 140 double-bookings a day.
incidents.constraint: Booking must stay one Postgres transaction under 50 ms.
incidents.question: What makes two overlapping bookings impossible?

choices.label: EXCLUDE constraint on room and time range

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Invariant enforced by the database, not by application checks.

choices.resultBody: An EXCLUDE USING gist constraint on room_id with equality and the booking range with overlap makes the database reject overlapping rows regardless of isolation level. The losing transaction gets an error and the UI offers the next free slot. Double-bookings drop to 0 for a GiST index and about 1 ms per insert.

choices.label: Re-check for overlapping bookings right before the INSERT
choices.resultBody: Under snapshot isolation the second check reads the same snapshot, and even outside it, two requests checking within the same 5 ms both see no row. This is write skew: neither transaction touches a row the other wrote. Double-bookings only drop to 120 a day.

choices.label: Track booked slots in Redis and check there first
choices.resultBody: The Redis check-then-set is another read-then-write race across two systems, and after a rolled-back transaction Redis and Postgres disagree. Double-bookings fall to 60 a day, and 2% of free slots now show as taken.

hints: Each transaction's check is correct on its own snapshot.
Neither transaction writes a row the other one read.
Can the database itself refuse overlapping time ranges?

incidents.title: New password rejected right after a reset
incidents.brief: Keyhold resets the password on the primary, then redirects to login, which checks the hash on a replica lagging 1-3 s. 11% of resets fail the first login, and 3 failures trigger a lockout.
incidents.constraint: Replicas carry 70k profile reads/s; login is only 400 req/s.
incidents.question: Where should the login check read the credential from?

choices.label: Check credentials on the primary; profiles stay on replicas

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Strong reads for the small security-critical path, replicas for the bulk.

choices.resultTitle: Logins see the new password at once
choices.resultBody: Credential checks are only 400 req/s, a rounding error for the primary, which goes from 52% to 54% CPU. Every login now sees the just-committed hash, first-login failures after a reset drop to 0, and the 70k profile reads/s stay on replicas.

choices.label: Auto-retry a failed login once after a 2-second pause
choices.resultBody: Each failed attempt still increments the lockout counter before the retry, so a user who also mistypes once reaches 3 failures and gets locked out. Lockouts rise to 2,600 a day, and genuine wrong-password attempts now take 2 s longer.

choices.label: Cache password hashes in Redis for 10 minutes per user
choices.resultBody: Logins get faster, but the cache now holds the pre-reset hash for up to 10 minutes: the new password fails and the old, possibly stolen one still works. The security team blocks the release.

hints: Only a tiny fraction of traffic touches credentials.
A security check that reads stale data is a correctness bug, not a UX glitch.
Is the primary really too busy for 400 extra reads per second?

incidents.title: Comment count goes 41, 38, 41 on refresh
incidents.brief: Threadly's mobile app spreads each GET across 3 replicas lagging 0.2 s, 1.5 s and 9 s. On hot threads, replies appear, vanish and reappear as users refresh.
incidents.constraint: Replicas must keep serving 60k reads/s; the primary cannot absorb them.
incidents.question: What stops one user's view from going backwards in time?

choices.label: Pin each session to one replica via consistent hash

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Monotonic reads per session; staleness itself is unchanged.

choices.resultBody: Each session now hashes to one replica, so successive reads never jump to an older snapshot; rewinds fall from 7% to about 0.1%, mostly during replica failover. Cost: load spreads less evenly, and users pinned to the 9 s replica still see older, though monotonic, data.

choices.label: Route every read to the primary until replicas catch up
choices.resultBody: The primary was sized for writes plus replication, not 60k reads/s. Its CPU pegs at 98%, p95 jumps to 1.4 s, and write latency degrades for every user.

choices.label: Put a 30-second CDN cache in front of every thread read
choices.resultBody: The cache hides churn between refreshes, but each 30 s refill pulls from a random replica; when a refill lands on the 9 s-lag one, the count still jumps backwards for every user on that POP.

hints: The data eventually converges; the problem is the order users see it in.
Consecutive refreshes can land on replicas with very different lag.
What if one user's reads always followed the same replication stream?

incidents.title: Viral video's like count jumps backwards
incidents.brief: A Clipster video goes viral at 3,000 likes/s. The API reads the count, adds 1, and writes it back, so concurrent requests overwrite each other: 12% of likes are lost and the count jumps backwards.
incidents.constraint: The count may lag a few seconds, but no like may be lost.
incidents.question: How do you count 3,000 likes/s on one video without losing any?

choices.label: Atomic increments spread across 32 counter shard rows

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Exact totals with a few seconds of display lag.

choices.resultTitle: Every like counted, no hot row
choices.resultBody: Each like runs UPDATE ... SET n = n + 1 on one of 32 shard rows picked at random, so every increment is atomic and lock waits spread 32 ways. Reads sum the 32 rows and cache the total for 2 s. Lost likes fall to 0 and DB CPU drops to 60%. Cost: displayed counts are up to 2 s old.

choices.label: SELECT FOR UPDATE on the row before each increment
choices.resultTitle: Likes queue behind one row lock
choices.resultBody: No likes are lost, but all 3,000 req/s now serialize on a single row lock held for a full round trip each. Lock waits pile up, p99 reaches 2.8 s, and the connection pool runs dry, failing likes on other videos too.

choices.label: Optimistic version check, retrying the like on conflict
choices.resultTitle: A retry storm on the hot row
choices.resultBody: At 3,000 writes/s on one row almost every attempt conflicts, so each like retries 5 to 10 times. Database load multiplies, CPU pegs at 99%, and requests that exhaust their retries drop 20% of likes.

hints: Read, add one, write back is not one operation.
Even an atomic increment on one row makes every request wait for the same lock.
What if the count lived in several rows that are summed on read?

incidents.title: Two tabs save, one edit silently vanishes
incidents.brief: On Wikidocs, 3% of page saves overwrite a concurrent edit. Both tabs read version 17, edit, and write the whole page back; the later write wins and nobody is warned.
incidents.constraint: Editing sessions last up to 10 minutes, so holding locks while a page is open is not acceptable.
incidents.question: What makes the second save notice it is based on stale data?

choices.label: Compare-and-set on the version number, 409 on mismatch

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Optimistic concurrency: no locks, but conflicts surface to users.

choices.resultBody: The second save's UPDATE ... WHERE version = 17 now matches zero rows, so the API returns 409 and shows a merge view; lost edits drop from 3% to 0. Cost: about 3% of saves need a manual merge, and every client must send the version it read.

choices.label: Pessimistic row lock held while the page is open
choices.resultBody: Locks held through 10-minute editing sessions pile up; 18% of page opens now wait or time out, and abandoned tabs keep pages locked until the 15-minute lease expires.

choices.label: Last-write-wins with tightly synced server timestamps
choices.resultBody: Tighter clocks only make it more predictable which save wins; the losing tab's changes are still discarded without a warning, so 3% of saves keep vanishing.

hints: Nothing crashed; one write simply replaced another.
Both writers based their change on version 17.
Make the write succeed only if the row is still what the writer read.

incidents.title: Replies show up before the question
incidents.brief: Threadr shards comments across 8 partitions, each replicating to APAC independently. A reply can land 2 s before its parent, so 4% of APAC readers see answers to questions that don't exist yet.
incidents.constraint: Partitions must replicate independently; one global log caps writes at 5k/s.
incidents.question: How do readers never see a reply without its parent?

choices.label: Replicas hold a reply until its parent is visible

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Causal consistency: dependencies ordered, unrelated writes still concurrent.

choices.resultBody: Each reply now records its parent's ID and version as a causal dependency. APAC buffers a reply until that dependency has been applied, usually under 500 ms, then makes it visible. Orphans drop to 0 with no global ordering. Cost: some replies appear up to 2 s later, and the buffer needs monitoring.

choices.label: Sort each thread by wall-clock timestamp on read
choices.resultBody: Sorting reorders whatever has arrived, but a reply whose parent hasn't replicated still renders alone, and 200 ms of clock skew between writers puts some replies above their parents. Orphans fall only from 4% to 3.5%.

choices.label: Route every comment through one global sequencer
choices.resultBody: A single totally ordered log does fix causality, but every comment now takes a round trip to one region and throughput caps at 5k writes/s. Peak traffic of 9k writes/s queues up and APAC write latency climbs to 400 ms.

hints: The data isn't wrong; it arrives in the wrong order.
Only writes that depend on each other need ordering.
What if a reply carried a note about what must be visible first?

incidents.title: Sneaker drop fails at payment for sold-out sizes
incidents.brief: During a SoleDrop release, product pages read stock from replicas 3 s behind at 150k req/s. Shoppers see 'in stock' after a size sells out, and 30% of checkouts fail at the payment step.
incidents.constraint: The primary handles 6k req/s and cannot serve 150k browse reads.
incidents.question: Which reads need the truth, and which can be stale?

choices.label: Browse from replicas; atomic stock reserve before payment

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Strong where money moves, eventual where people browse.

choices.resultTitle: Failures move to a cheap, early step
choices.resultBody: Product pages keep reading replicas and show 'low stock' below 20 units. Checkout's first step runs UPDATE stock SET n = n - 1 WHERE n > 0 on the primary, about 2k req/s at peak, so buyers learn instantly and payment only runs on a reserved unit. Payment-stage failures fall to 0.5%; reservations expire after 10 minutes.

choices.label: Serve product pages from the primary during sneaker drops
choices.resultBody: 150k req/s lands on a primary sized for 6k. CPU pegs at 100%, reads and checkouts queue together, and the release page times out for everyone within a minute.

choices.label: Cache stock in Redis, refreshed from replicas each second
choices.resultTitle: Faster stale data is still stale
choices.resultBody: Pages get faster, but the cache copies a 3 s-old replica every second, so pages trail the truth by 3-4 s. Checkouts still reach payment for sold-out sizes; failures fall only to 26%.

hints: Not every read in this flow has the same stakes.
A slightly wrong 'in stock' badge is harmless; a charge for nothing is not.
Which single step could check and claim a unit atomically?

incidents.title: Stolen phone's session survives logout
incidents.brief: Vaultly's gateways validate 1-hour JWTs locally at 50k req/s. When a customer reports a stolen phone and logs out everywhere, the thief's token keeps working for up to 60 minutes.
incidents.constraint: Revocation must take effect within 10 s; the session DB handles 3k req/s.
incidents.question: How do you revoke a stateless token fast without a DB call per request?

choices.label: Push revoked token IDs to each gateway's in-memory denylist

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Bounded revocation lag of seconds with no per-request DB call.

choices.resultBody: Logout-everywhere writes each token's jti to a revocation table and publishes it on pub/sub. Every gateway keeps a small in-memory set until the token's natural expiry, so checks stay local at about 1 µs and revocation lands in under 2 s. Cost: a restarting gateway must load the list before it serves traffic.

choices.label: Check every request's token against the session database
choices.resultBody: Revocation is instant, but 50k checks/s hit a session DB sized for 3k. CPU pegs at 99%, gateway p99 goes from 8 ms to 1.2 s, and failed checks start logging honest customers out.

choices.label: Shorten access tokens to 30 s and lean on refresh tokens
choices.resultTitle: Refresh traffic swamps the session DB
choices.resultBody: Revocation now takes up to 30 s, still missing the 10 s target, and every client refreshes 120 times an hour. Refresh calls hit the session DB at 13k req/s, over four times its capacity, and logins start failing.

hints: A signed token is valid until it expires, by design.
Revoked tokens are a tiny set compared to all live tokens.
Gateways could learn about revocations instead of asking about every token.

incidents.title: Two workers both think they own the ledger lock
incidents.brief: Ledgerly's billing worker froze 14 s in a GC pause. Its 10 s lease expired, a second worker took over, then the first woke up and kept writing. 212 invoices double-posted.
incidents.constraint: Leases stay; the ledger database is the only place both writers meet.
incidents.question: What stops the stale lock holder's writes from landing?

choices.label: Fencing token per lease; ledger rejects lower tokens

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Safety moves to the storage layer; clients must propagate tokens.

choices.resultBody: Each lease grant carries an increasing token (33, then 34), and the ledger refuses any write tagged lower than the highest it has seen, so Worker A's post-pause writes fail. Cost: every write path must carry the token, and storage needs a conditional-write check.

choices.label: Shorten the lease TTL from 10 s to 3 s with faster renewals
choices.resultBody: A 14 s GC pause still outlives a 3 s lease, and ordinary network blips now trigger spurious failovers; double-posts only drop to 150 while leader churn triples.

choices.label: Have each worker recheck its lease right before writing
choices.resultBody: Worker A checks, sees a valid lease, then stalls before its write lands; the check-then-act gap still lets 180 invoices double-post, because the ledger has no idea the lease moved.

hints: The first worker never learned it had been replaced.
Any check the worker makes itself can go stale during a pause.
The ledger needs a way to tell an old lock holder from a new one.

incidents.title: Quote screens show prices up to 40 s old
incidents.brief: TradeLite serves 120k quote reads/s from 6 async replicas. Lag is usually 300 ms, but during a bulk import two replicas fall 40 s behind and customers trade on stale prices.
incidents.constraint: The contract caps quote staleness at 2 s, and the primary cannot serve 120k reads/s.
incidents.question: How do you enforce the 2 s bound without moving reads to the primary?

choices.label: Pull replicas lagging more than 2 s out of routing

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Bounded staleness by exclusion; capacity drops while replicas catch up.

choices.resultBody: The router polls replication lag every 250 ms and drains any replica past 2 s; stale-quote reads fall from 31% to about 0.3%. Cost: four replicas now carry all 120k reads/s at 86% CPU, so you need headroom or a seventh replica.

choices.label: Add two more async replicas to spread the read load
choices.resultBody: The two new replicas replay the same bulk import and fall 35 s behind as well; the router still sends them a share of traffic, so 30% of reads remain over the 2 s bound.

choices.label: Cache quotes in Redis with a 5-second TTL per symbol
choices.resultTitle: The cache breaks the SLA by itself
choices.resultBody: A 5 s TTL alone can serve quotes older than the 2 s bound, and cache fills from the 40 s-behind replicas lock stale prices in; over-bound reads rise to 38%.

hints: Most replicas are fine; a couple are far behind.
The SLA is about the age of the data, not the speed of the response.
Decide per replica, based on how far behind it currently is.

incidents.title: Cart forgets the item added seconds ago
incidents.brief: ShopNest's cart store keeps N=3 replicas with W=1 writes and R=1 reads for speed. After a node blip, 4% of cart reads miss an item added seconds earlier.
incidents.constraint: Reads and writes must both keep working with one replica down; there is no single leader.
incidents.question: Which quorum setting guarantees a read sees the latest acknowledged write?

choices.label: Write quorum W=2 and read quorum R=2 with N=3

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Overlapping quorums trade a few ms of latency for read-after-write.

choices.resultBody: With R + W = 4 > N = 3 on strict (not sloppy) quorums, every read set shares at least one replica with the last acknowledged write, and one node can still fail. Missing items drop to about 0; cost: p95 rises from 12 ms to 19 ms waiting for the second replica.

choices.label: Write W=3 to all replicas, keep reads at R=1
choices.resultTitle: Writes fail whenever a node dips
choices.resultBody: R=1 plus W=3 does overlap, but every write now needs all three replicas; during the next 90 s node restart every add-to-cart fails, breaking the one-node-down requirement.

choices.label: Keep R=1, W=1 and retry reads that look empty
choices.resultBody: A cart missing one item is not empty, so the retry rarely fires; when it does, it asks another single replica that may also be behind. Misses only fall from 4% to 3.5%.

hints: Each write is acknowledged after reaching just one of three replicas.
A single-replica read may pick a different node than the write did.
Make the nodes you read from always intersect the nodes you wrote to.

incidents.title: One replica falls 40 s behind after a cost cut
incidents.brief: Bookly moved Replica C to a burstable 2-vCPU instance to save $300/month. Its CPU credits ran out; WAL replay pins it at 98% and lag hit 40 s. 9% of reads are stale.
incidents.constraint: The primary and the other two replicas replay fine at about 30% CPU; the fix must ship today.
incidents.question: What brings Replica C back in line with its peers?

choices.label: Upsize Replica C back to the 8-vCPU class its peers use

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Gives back the $300/month saving; replication behaves exactly as it did last week.

choices.resultTitle: Replica C catches up in minutes
choices.resultBody: On a non-burstable 8-vCPU instance WAL replay runs at 30% CPU again, the 40 s backlog drains in about four minutes, and stale reads fall to 0.2%. The design was never wrong; the box was. Cost: the $300/month saving is gone.

choices.label: Add session LSN tokens so reads skip lagging replicas
choices.resultTitle: Reads dodge C, but C never recovers
choices.resultBody: The router change takes two days to build and review, missing today's deadline. Once live, A and B absorb C's share at 45% CPU, while C stays out of credits and its lag keeps growing, so you are paying for a replica nobody can read.

choices.label: Put Replica C on synchronous replication so it cannot lag
choices.resultTitle: Every commit now waits on the slow box
choices.resultBody: Synchronous commit makes the primary wait for Replica C to flush each WAL record, and C is still CPU-starved. Booking write p99 jumps from 9 ms to 1.8 s and checkouts time out, while C's CPU stays pinned.

hints: Only one replica is behind, and it is the one that changed last week.
Look at what Replica C is short of, not at how reads are routed.
A burstable instance with no CPU credits cannot keep up with WAL replay.
